Let me take you back on a journey, about 24 years ago. A teenage me, browsing through a PC magazine looking for parts to build my stepfather a new rig. My stepfather was living in Phoenix at the time and we had settled on going to this small PC shop just outside of downtown I believe. There we looked at acrylic cases for the build when something piqued my interest in the store add that I hadn't noticed before. There was a set of headphones that claimed to have subwoofers in them. They used a single AA battery in a case in-line with the cord and had a small thumb dial to adjust the bass. They were on special for $10.99 down from $19.99. With a look of excitement, I turned to my stepfather and asked if he would be willing to purchase them for me. He agreed happily, stating that these would be a form of payment for my labor in building his PC.

Needless to say, I could not wait to try them out with my CD Walkman and some hip-hop/rap music. Now, at the time, i dont bleieve these headphones were skullcandy brand. The band was plastic and flimsy, so were the swivels for the ear cups but I'll never forget the first time the bass came on and I could feel it on my ears. The audio quality was average but it was just the way I could experience the bass that made them wonderful. Expectedly, those headphones were not long lived. The band broke about 6 months after constant use but the drivers were still in working order so sometimes I would just hold them up to my ears and enjoyed them.

Fast forward about 8 years, I discovered skullcandy. While browsing through their site, I saw the original Crushers. The design was almost identical to the ones I used to have except the band was slightly different, a little more beafy but still looked like they wouldn't last. Wanting the experience again but knowing that the quality might end up the same, I held off on buying those and ended up with a pair of Hesh in Snow Camo. The Hesh were good, standard 40mm drivers but they were power hungry. You really couldn't enjoy the full quality of the drivers unless they were plugged into a PC with a good sound card, a studio Amp or a small in-line Amp along with an ipod, phone etc. With the experience from the Hesh, I figured the Crushers would suffer from the same symptoms so I waited.

When I saw the first Bluetooth Crushers, I knew it was a step in the right direction for the line. When I read through the reviews, it gave me high hopes but I was still on the fence and stuck to my Beats Solo that I'd had for years. Now, finally, I decided to take the plunge with these ANC Crushers. For what these are, I am not disappointed in the least. Those original headphones just really adjusted the vibration with little affect to the audible bass but these ANC Crushers are everything I hoped for. The mids and highs are clear and the bass is powerful. Now, these may not be for everyone, the lowest bass adjustment might still be too much for some but for what I wanted them for, they are everything.

review_content:
Let's review, I have the first gen skull candy crushers and I loved them. However the first get ear pads got worn down due to me using them so much. As I was searching I found these and thought I'd give it a shot.

They are pricey. But for what you get it's outstanding. You get a custom audio profile which allows the music to tuned to your own sound preference. It has a built in skull candy voice assistant for hands free features. Solid buttons on the side which are nice. They fit your ears! The first gen tended to put a bit of pressure on my ears which made it uncomfortable at times but these are light weight and pain free.

Let's go into the audiophile people. For those who are maniacs about how music sounds, I can't understand the audiophiles but this headset makes very clear music, amazing sound, great feeling and built in equalizer in the app to let you adjust the music to your preference.

It works with a mic as well. I constantly use the headset for phone calls. The multipoint pairing is great. I could be watching a movie on my tablet and get a phone call and it'll automatically pause my movie and switch directly to my phone and let me take the call.

The appearance is nice. The case and everything is solid and it comes with a semi hard carrying case to keep everything in with USB C fast charging cord and 3mm jack for old CD players or mp3 players which is awesome because I actually miss the corded days.

Beyond that the headset has a 50 hour battery life which is outstanding and it's more durable than the 1st generation.

Now for the kicker. If you love bass in your music and want that subwoofer feel on your ears then buy this hands down. It will shake your head and give you that loud noise you want. But you always have the option to turn it off.

Overall I'm pleased, even getting it at full price is worth it however I got it cheaper on a Labor Day sale and continue to use it regularly everyday.

(Ps. It says it was designed for Apple products however it works with Android and the features work amazing with Android )

App? Most products like this has apps nowadays, and this is no exception. But what I wasn’t expecting was the ability to be able to pair to multiple devices. product_review_title: Pretty darn good for the sale price under $150.
review_content:
I ordered the Crusher AC2 and the Sony XM5 to compare side by side. $150 vs $420. The Crusher are heavier, but I assume that is part of having double the battery life. Great build quality and great sound. Those who say you cannot turn off the Crusher base do not know how these work. The wheel is also a button. If you press you get 20, 50, and 80 base on a 05 to 100 scale. The awesome app that comes with these lets you change those presets or turn the bass boost off completely. You can spin the wheel to get any number from 05 to 100. So yes, you do need the app to turn off bass boost completely, but I liked the sound of these a lot. The Sony XM5 is much lighter and has bigger ear cups. Certainly more comfortable for long wear.

The biggest difference is the sound canceling. The Cursher cuts 50% and the Sony XM5 maybe 70%. With no music, you hear kitchen vent noise through both, but less on Sony (best I could simulate airplane noise and it was maybe a little louder than an airplane). With music playing I turned the sound down on the Sony to where I could just hear the vent and then went one click louder. The Crusher at that volume cut out 98% of the vent noise and I actually like the sound turned up another click and then you didn't hear the vent...almost. It felt like some higher frequencies were maybe there a bit. But there wasn't $250 more value in the Sony for me.

While I decided to keep the Crusher AC2 and send back the Sony, the next day I tried to use the Crusher with my Samsung TV and they would connect and disconnect immediately. I never tried to solve this problem when I couldn't get any human support from Skull Candy...and so these went back too.

As a fellow bass enjoyer, the best I can describe the bass sounding is if you were to take the subwoofer rattle from a good car speaker setup and put it right up against both sides of your head.

However in terms of sound quality, the headphones aren’t bad. The headphones cut out some of the mids and high-mids which kinda just muddies every sound except base together, kinda reminds me of how some anker soundcore earbuds sound. Dont get me wrong, the sound isnt bad, but not the best quality you can get in a 200$ pair of Bluetooth headphones. Most likely, ur not buying these headphones for top notch audio.

Noice cancellation is not good. The headphones dont really cancel that much noise. No where near as good as Sony’s or apple’s noise cancellation. The transparency mode also barely does anything. I found I have to lower volume all the way down to 20% to hear a normal conversation.

product_review_title: Easy to Listen and Pleasing, but…
review_content:
I am an audiophile and music is one of my passions in life. I do own a few high end speakers and headphones: Focal Utopia, Focal Bathys, Monolith M1070 Planar, AirPod Pro 2, couple of Bose QC, and Bose NC700 among my current collection, and I’ve tested many more over the years. After reading so many good reviews and seeing people are comparing this against other ordinary headphones, I decided to order one and see how it stands against the Focal Bathys that currently is just a bit more money.

The history of the bacterial processed cellulose drivers Bowers used in Px7 intrigued me which are the closest you can get to the legendary Sony MDR-R10 from the 80s that did cost $2500 per pair back then and would be $6500 adjusted in today’s money, so Px7 S3 price is well worth the test!

Unboxing and First Impression:

Box was easy to open. You get the sliding cover out, remove the bottom of the package perforated paper sealing, and you can remove the top half. Unboxing and holding the headphones all screams quality, and the low profile and smaller size against Bathys made my mouth drooling. Bathys is way bigger. On your head you actually can feel the big size and weight, which is not comfortable for longer use. Px7 S3 is much slimmer and lighter which is amazing. Overall, more comfortable.

Connecting to Bluetooth asked to get the app and set up was easy in 3-5 min creating an account. It had 64% battery.

Sound Quality:

I have mixed feelings. Openness, separation, soundstage, and clarity definitely goes to Focal, but lower end extension, smoothness, noise cancellation, and overall loudness goes to Bowers that has a pleasing profile. I would describe the sound of Bowers as transparent and coherent, and Focal as exciting. If I can have only one pair, I would go with Focal for the better clarity and being better on more tracks, but Bowers is better than most headphones like Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra. However, Bowers boominess at times bothers me, and Focal is better with most vocals male or female.

Now keep in mind, Bowers has a new 5 band equalizer, and I could mimic Focal’s profile by reversing the V shaped sound of Px7 to some extent by adding +1.5 to band between LO and MID, +3 for MID, and +1.5 for between MID and HI: [0, +1.5, +3, +1.5, 0].

After everything, still more songs sound better on Bathys while some do better on Px7S3. Bathys is like the singer is singing in front of you, and Bowers is like you’re listening to a hi-res recording with more vibrations from your subwoofer. I should mention that Px7S3 can get very loud thanks to new dedicated amps, but it gets distorted. When you increase Focal’s volume, clarity is there but things scream very brightly at you. Neither one is great at highest volumes.

Maybe the better comparison is between Bathys and the upcoming Px8 S2 which was mentioned in the users manual, but for the current Px8 (version 1) with carbon fiber drivers, I think Focal has an edge.

Conclusion:

If you’ve a pair of high-end headphones like Focal Bathys, you don’t need to upgrade for better sound quality. However, if you need like more portability and better ANC, then Bowers Px7 S3 is a good choice with a nice history on the drivers material. It is definitely better than consumer grade headphones like Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra. As for me, if I didn’t have three pairs of Bose, I would keep this one for travel and commute and keep the Focal at home. I am just not sure if I need another $500 pair.

*** Update Regarding In-Flight ANC:

My first air travel with these headphones was a little underwhelming. During takeoff, I kept hearing these horrible pulsating noises, and on air, every time I turned my head towards the window, I heard more humming engine noise. I even had a chance to update the firmware to the latest, but it didn’t help with ANC. I will try again on my return flight again and hopefully I will have a better seat.

Update Return Flight:

Okay, so the noises are there for ANC. No matter which side of the plane you are sitting, left or right, turning your head to the right will increase the humming noises. So if you are in an F-seat near the window, looking out increases the noise, and if you are on an A-seat, still looking right to the isle will do the same. Must be an uneven microphone array positioning issue that only does this when turning right. Take off noise is still there too. The best way I can describe it is when you roll down the window driving fast on a highway. The same throbbing annoying wind buffeting sound happens during take off.

product_review_title: 3-MONTH UPDATE: great headphones but far from perfect
review_content:
After 90 days of daily use and direct comparison with the Bose QC Ultra and Sony WH-1000XM6, I’ve found that the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 is a headphone of "highs and lows"—literally and figuratively. If you are looking for the "perfect" all-rounder, this might not be it, but for a specific type of listener, it’s unbeatable.

​Build Quality & Aesthetics (3-Month Update):
​Reviewers often call the B&W build "unrivaled," but I’d call it a side-grade to Bose. While the earcup housings use premium metal (Bose uses plastic), the B&W hinges are plastic (Bose uses metal). Sony’s XM6 remains the most "plastic" of the bunch.
​-Durability: After 3 months, the white finish on the headphones is surprisingly pristine.
​-The Case: This is the weak link. The white fabric case is a magnet for grime and scuffs. It looks "used" very quickly, unlike the headphones themselves.

​Sound Quality: A V-Shaped Masterclass
​If you enjoy a V or U-shaped sound signature, you will love these. They offer the best bass of the three flagships—punchy and deep without becoming muddy or drowning out the mids.
​-The "Big But" (Wired Use): When using USB-C, there is a massive volume discrepancy. On iOS (iPhone/iPad), they sound fantastic and plenty loud. On Android, the volume ceiling is significantly lower. If you’re an Android user planning on wired listening, keep this power-output bug in mind.

​Noise Cancellation & Transparency
​-ANC: Average at best. It’s simply not in the same league as the "dead silence" provided by Sony or Bose. It’s fine for basic office noise, but it won't vanish a plane engine.
​-Transparency: Excellent. It feels natural and airy, easily one of the best implementations on the market.

​Call Quality & Voice Isolation:
​I’ve used these for dozens of work calls, and the voice isolation is quite decent. It carves out your voice well in noisy rooms. However, the Sony XM6 still wins here. Sony’s support for LE Audio (on compatible devices) makes voices sound clearer and more high-fidelity than the Px7 S3.

​Comfort & Controls:
​-Comfort: These are the least comfortable of the three for me. I feel a hotspot on the crown of my head after about an hour or two. The Bose Ultra remains the undisputed king of long-term wear.
​-Controls: I prefer Sony’s touch shortcuts, but the B&W physical buttons are a solid second place—much more reliable and tactile than the frustrating volume slider on the Bose.

​App & UX:
​The app is basic, neat, and straightforward. You get a 3-band EQ which, while simple, is enough to refine that already excellent sound signature.

​The Verdict
​Choose the Px7 S3 if: You prioritize music "soul" and bass quality over everything else, and you want a headphone that looks like a piece of high-end jewelry.
​Choose the Competition if: You need world-class ANC (Sony/Bose), all-day physical comfort (Bose), or the jack of all trades (Sony xm6).

​PROS:
​-Addictive, punchy bass that doesn't bleed.
​-Premium metal earcup construction.
​-Reliable physical buttons.
​-Natural Transparency mode.

​CONS:
​-Headband pressure during long sessions.
​-​Sub-par ANC compared to Sony/Bose.
​-Low USB-C volume on Android.
​-The white case gets dirty instantly.

review_content:
I bought the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 because I wanted “good sound,” but what I got feels more like my ears got upgraded without my permission.

First impression: these headphones mean business. The build feels premium like the kind of thing you don’t casually toss onto a couch unless you want to feel judged by an inanimate object. They’ve got that sleek, “I listen to jazz and make important decisions” energy, even if you’re actually just listening to questionable playlists and avoiding emails.

Now let’s talk soundstage, because wow. This is where things get a little ridiculous (in the best way). The sound is so wide and immersive that I briefly checked if my room had expanded. Instruments aren’t just playing they’re existing in space with intention. I had one moment where I turned my head thinking someone called my name… it was just a hi-hat. Respectfully, that’s not normal behavior for headphones.

Bass is clean and controlled, not the “I swallowed a subwoofer” kind of bass, but more like “this sound engineer has their life together.” Mids are crisp, vocals sit perfectly, and highs are detailed without turning into tiny ice picks in your ears.

Noise cancellation is excellent too. It doesn’t just reduce noise it politely removes the outside world and says, “they’re busy right now.” I could finally focus, which is dangerous because I started hearing how bad my old headphones really were.

Comfort-wise, they’re very wearable. I forgot I had them on until I tried to order coffee out loud and realized I wasn’t on a call.

Downsides? Well, once you hear your music like this, there’s no going back. You’ll start judging every other audio device in your life like it personally betrayed you. Also, you may develop the habit of sitting very still just to “experience the soundstage,” which is a slippery slope into audiophile territory.

Final verdict: The Px7 S3 delivers an absolutely massive, immersive soundstage with top-tier clarity and comfort. If you want headphones that make your music feel like it’s happening around you instead of just in your head, these are dangerously good. Just be warned you might start treating silence as “poorly mixed audio.”

With only two exceptions, it hasn’t been overly difficult for me to test ride a pair of either format without going out and purchasing a pair to keep.

As I consume reviews nearly as voraciously as I devour music, I have had my eye on the B&W Px7 S3 since their critically-acclaimed debut but put off a test run as I was happy with my current options. I wasn’t happy, turns out. Rather, primitive, naive to put it into hyperbole.

But in a measured vein, can’t recommend these highly enough. 10/10 full stars.

product_review_title: Great if audio quality is #1 priority, ok ANC, lots of bass
review_content:
Great detailed sound, decent ANC but not on the level of Sony/Bose/Apple. I find the ANC good enough; I don't really need the ANC tech that shuts out the entire world - and when I do I have an old pair of Sony xm4 earbuds that do it just fine. You will really only know if the ANC is for you if you try it, but Bowers' goal was clearly more to create a good listening environment; less to screen out all noise. You'll hear your music on a plane just fine. You won't be deaf to the rest of the universe.

I refunded a Sony xm6 pair and got these - am very happy. The bigger, deeper earcups are more comfy to me, and while I've heard some say the clamping force is excessive, I wanted to voice a contrary opinion and say I actually prefer it - the Sonys rely on gravity and the headband starts irritating the top of my head within 30 minutes; these I could wear all day.

In terms of sound, I prefer these to the Apple, Bose and Sony offerings at this price point. I get better clarity, a wider soundstage and generally a more detailed and immersive experience. I'm not a huge spatial audio aficionado, so the present lack of spatial audio and promise of adding it in a future update isn't really a concern for me, but a good stereo field provides plenty of detail. On classical recordings, I can hear so much detail that I'm catching page turns and chair creaks I've never noticed in my favorite recordings.

These phones are bass-heavy. If that's an issue, you've been warned. It doesn't distort or ruin the sound, but it's powerful.

The USB-C, 3.5mm and bluetooth audio connections all work well, though I might recommend a 3rd party USB-C cable if you're streaming audio from a gaming handheld with vibration - the included cable is firm enough that it transfers vibrations from the console to your ear, meaning you will hear a buzz when your Switch/SteamDeck/etc vibrates.

product_review_title: Almost Awesome, But A Noise Cancellation Nightmare
review_content: Incredibly comfortable, much more so than any other pair of Noise Cancelling Headphones I’ve tried (Sony XM4, 5, 6. Airpods Max) Sounds better than all the aforementioned headphones as well (subjectively, that is). The reason these get 3 stars despite mostly positives and why I will not be keeping them is because the noise cancellation is subpar AND the inability to control noise cancellation level/type either in app or on device. While on a 12 hour flight, I wanted to rest, but I learned that the “smart switching of noise cancellation” feature cannot be manually overridden and locked into one type. Thus, every time I would tilt my head to the side to rest, it would decide I no longer needed maximum noise cancellation, and suddenly all the engine noise would come through. This was unpredictable as well, sometimes I wouldn’t move at all and the noise cancellation would switch off. I’d have to cycle through the types (noise cancellation off, transparency, noise cancellation) to get it to return, usually for it to then switch to a lower level again automatically soon after. I could handle subpar noise cancellation, but this lack of user autonomy to choose what level you want and keep it there actually makes it a nightmarish failure.

review_content:
Have you ever wanted the perfect pair of headphones—premium quality, immersive sound, and all under $1,000? Have you dreamed of audio that makes you feel like you're sitting in an AMC IMAX theater? What if your headphones could connect to multiple devices at once, without constantly pairing and unpairing? And what if all this came in a sleek, high-end package?

Look no further—**these headphones are it**.

I've tried dozens—maybe even 20 or more—headphones and earbuds, each hyped as “the best” by some reviewer. I’ve dropped $300 to $400 on sets that turned out to be a disappointment. They check none of the real boxes—just loud, flat sound hyped by people who only care about footsteps in shooters or volume levels.

**These headphones are different.** They check every box and more.

They transform any movie, song, or game into a rich, crisp, cinematic experience—truly IMAX-level immersion. The search is over. You’ve made it.

Now, the PX8—this brand's flagship model—is supposed to be dropping soon, so that’s worth keeping an eye on. But in my opinion, **these outperform the PX8 S1 and the Sony XM6**, easily.

The ANC (Active Noise Cancellation) is very good—maybe not industry-best—but honestly, when you're immersed in great audio, that detail fades into the background. Call quality is rumored to be just okay, but I haven’t had a single issue.

**Final verdict? 10 out of 10. Perfect.**

If you too just like me are led to believe it’s pretty much non-existent, this couldn’t be further from the truth and I can’t stress this enough. Don’t let it stop you from buying these.

However, I must mention that comfort is a concern. Despite my average head size, these headphones feel quite tight during extended listening sessions. As far as ANC performance I give the Bose QC Ultra the edge. Not that the PC7 S3s ANC was bad, just not as good as the QC Ultras. However. review_content:
The Beats Studio Pro headphones present a solid upgrade from previous generations, particularly for those seeking quality sound and effective features. While they are marketed as renewed, I found that they performed just as well as new models, showcasing the durability and reliability of Beats' craftsmanship.

Sound Quality:
One notable aspect is the volume level, which is slightly lower than earlier versions. However, this doesn't detract significantly from the listening experience; it's still ample for most casual listeners. The sound profile remains rich, with a focus on bass that Beats fans will appreciate.

Noise Cancellation:
The noise cancellation is commendable, effectively blocking out ambient noise in quieter environments. However, in bustling places like malls, some external sounds can seep in if the music isn't turned up high enough. This is something to consider for those who plan to use them in noisy settings.

Transparency Mode:
The transparency mode is impressively good, allowing outside sounds to come through without compromising on audio quality. This feature is particularly useful for staying aware of your surroundings while enjoying music.

Comfort:
On the comfort front, the clamping force feels a bit strong. While the ear cups are designed to rest over your ears rather than fully enclose them, this can lead to discomfort during extended use. It may take some time to adjust, especially for users who prefer a looser fit.

Potential Bias:
It's important to acknowledge potential bias in this review. Given that these headphones were renewed, there may be variations in individual units, influencing performance and comfort. Additionally, my preferences in sound profile and use cases may not align with those of every potential buyer. While I found the headphones satisfactory, others might prioritize different features or experiences.

Overall, the Beats Studio Pro headphones are a solid choice for those looking for reliable performance and excellent features, particularly if you value transparency mode and solid sound quality. Just be mindful of the fit and volume levels based on your personal preferences.

review_content:
Everyone warned me not to buy Beats headphones: I was told they're badly made, they're uncomfortable, the sound quality isn't great for the price, and so on. But my friend had a pair, and I thought they looked great and felt great, and I had no issues with the sound, so I bought a pair. It was a big mistake.

After wearing them for a few hours, the top of my head started to hurt terribly, and I had to take them off. After a few weeks of wearing them each day, I had a permanent bruise-like feeling on the top of my head. Eventually I did some research, and bought a padded protector to wrap around the top. It didn't solve the problem entirely (they were still too tight around the ears), but it made them wearable. Unfortunately, my nice looking headphones now looked ridiculous.

And then, today, about one month out of the one-year warranty, the band just snaps. I had put no special pressure on them; I wasn't rough in the least. I handled them as I'd always handled them. I looked closely at the place where it snapped, and I see that, even though the internal band is made of metal, the place where the band meets the actual earpiece (where the hinge is) is just a couple of millimeters of plastic. So of course it broke: a piece of plastic being stretched on a daily basis isn't going to last very long.

So, basically, you're paying $200 for uncomfortable headphones that can't withstand a year of daily use. They sound fine, they connect fine, they look good, but they hurt to wear and they'll be fit for the trash can within a year.

product_review_title: I'm very pleased overall, but ANC only so-so.
product_attributes: Color: Navy; Size: One Size; Style: Studio Pro
review_content:
I bought this product because my ears get fatigued from AirPods (Pro) sometimes but I want to still listen to my audiobooks. I also wanted something for airplane trips. Sleeping with earbuds on the plane is painful and then I've had one or both fall out and roll under my seat or way back under someone else's seat, which is really gross. Even though they are a bit heavy, they are very comfortable. I have small ears, so these fit really well--right inside with no pressure on the cartilage. If you have big ears or a big head, I don't know. It might be worth a try anyway.

I love being able to control the volume on the device, unlike my AirPods where you have to pull out the phone to control the volume. I have a few cons though. I can't really wear these outside or for intense workouts because if I get sweaty, they slide around on my ears. My son would wear these while mowing the lawn and I thought I could too, but it didn't work well. I got sweaty and they slid around and broke the audio seal, letting in a lot of background noise. And they don't have the noise cancelling capability that AirPods do. When I mow with the AirPods, I only hear a little background noise. With these headphones I still hear a lot of background noise. Same thing goes for using the vacuum cleaner and even at the car wash. With AirPods, I hear nothing. With these, I have to turn the volume way up to drown out the background noise. This concerns me for flights because I want everything tuned out except my audiobook or maybe a movie.

But the Bluetooth range is awesome!! With my AirPods, the phone has to be in fairly close proximity or it will lose connectivity. With these headphones I can go way down the street away from my phone and they will still be connected! I will have my phone plugged in inside the basement and go all the way out to the mailbox or to the neighbor's house and still be connected. It's like a dream! I can go places around my home and property with these headphones I couldn't go before (with the phone left inside somewhere).

They also are comparable to AirPods in regards to phone calls, Google meet, or FaceTime. I haven't worn them long enough to determine battery life. My hope is they will last on a cross country or international flight with constant use. AirPods definitely don't.

So these headphones have not replaced my AirPods, but I certainly prefer them in certain situations over others. I'm happy I bought them!
